brief.topic: When Two Backups Share One Weakness

s01: Two backups can be less protection than they look.
Imagine two toy components. Either one can keep a system working.
Each has a one in four chance of failing during our chosen period.
First, suppose their failures are independent.
We can picture each component with four equally likely states. One state means failure.
Pair every state of the first with every state of the second.
That makes sixteen equally likely pairs.
Only one pair has both components fail.
The other fifteen leave at least one working.
So the chance the system works is fifteen out of sixteen.
Now change just one assumption. Both components fail on exactly the same event.
When that shared event occurs, both are lost together.
For either component, the failure chance is still one quarter.
But the pair also fails one time in four. The extra component has added no protection.
The difference is not the number of boxes. It is how their failures are related.
Independent failures let us multiply one quarter by one quarter.
Shared failure does not permit that multiplication.
Real backups may share power, location, or a software mistake.
Our numbers are a toy example, not measured failure rates.
When you see a second path, ask whether the same event can close both.

scenes.narration:
Two backups can be less protection than they look. Imagine two toy components. Either one can keep a system working. Each has a one in four chance of failing during our chosen period.

First, suppose their failures are independent. We can picture each component with four equally likely states. One state means failure. Pair every state of the first with every state of the second. That makes sixteen equally likely pairs.

Only one pair has both components fail. The other fifteen leave at least one working. So the chance the system works is fifteen out of sixteen.

Now change just one assumption. Both components fail on exactly the same event. When that shared event occurs, both are lost together. For either component, the failure chance is still one quarter. But the pair also fails one time in four. The extra component has added no protection.

The difference is not the number of boxes. It is how their failures are related. Independent failures let us multiply one quarter by one quarter. Shared failure does not permit that multiplication.

Real backups may share power, location, or a software mistake. Our numbers are a toy example, not measured failure rates. When you see a second path, ask whether the same event can close both.
